speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Azmoon Ahmad raised pertinent issues about AVs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As we all noted, AV technology is not yet mature.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In answer to Mr Dennis Tan, these drivers have a Class 3 licence and they have no demerit points.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This need for a safety driver can be waived after the AV developers have proven the competency of their AVs to LTA's full satisfaction of navigating our infrastructure and roads.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Third, trials are allowed to start only on lightly used roads like the one we have at one-north.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: When the AVs are able to demonstrate higher competencies, they will be allowed to trial in more complex environments, including some of our public roads.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The proposed RTA provisions will give LTA the flexibility to impose additional requirements or amend requirements, as the need arises, because, in many of these trials, there may be unforeseen circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Therefore, giving LTA the flexibility is the sensible thing to do.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Azmoon Ahmad and Mr Melvin Yong asked about the legal implications and many potential liability issues when AVs are involved in road accidents.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Henry Kwek also asked if the insurance industry is being consulted.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: LTA is studying these complex issues, together with representatives from the AV, motor, legal and insurance industries, and this is part of the work set up under MOT's Committee on Autonomous Road Transport for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This is an 18-member strong Committee comprising senior members in Singapore public agencies, public sector and some global organisations.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In the meantime, LTA has been discussing these issues with foreign counterparts that have also similar test-beds.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: On liability, the traditional basis of claims for negligence may not work so well − as Mr Dennis Tan has said − where there is no driver in control of a vehicle.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: When presented with novel technologies, Courts often try to draw analogies to legal constructs for other existing technologies.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In the case of AVs, the Courts have autopilot systems for airplanes and autopilot navigational systems for maritime vessels, and product liability law to draw references from.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But having said this, these are early days yet.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: A lot of detailed studies will have to be done, including the point raised by Mr Dennis Tan on the future framework, whether this class of vehicles requires licensing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I think this will be an area to be studied.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad and Mr Melvin Yong asked about the issue of certification.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Indeed, this is the reason LTA, together with JTC Corp, in partnership with NTU, have started a Centre for Excellence for Testing and Research of Autonomous Vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This organisation called CETRAN will spearhead the development of AV testing requirements.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked if our road and public transport network can accommodate AVs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: A key requirement of the trials initiated by LTA is that the AVs can operate on our existing roads with minimal supporting structure.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Globally, the industry is also gearing towards such infrastructure-light AVs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: So, the short answer is yes, the trials will guide the AVs towards infrastructure-light modifications.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked what the penalties are for AV trial participants who do not buy the appropriate insurance or fail to place the stipulated security deposit with LTA.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Companies or individuals which do not or fail to do so will not be issued a test licence to conduct AV trials.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if LTA would consider mandating that trial data be transmitted real-time to LTA's Intelligent Transport System Centre.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Currently, the answer is that trial participants are not required to do so, but I take that point and we are already requiring LTA to get this system set up for real-time transmission in the longer term for all the AV trials.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Melvin Yong also asked if AVs would be subjected to COE should there be an increase in AVs being trialled on our roads.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In the longer term, when AV technology is mature and deployed widely in public, there does not seem to be any reason why we should exempt them from our COE system.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We will review the policy at an appropriate point in time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We have set a relatively high bar to deter acts of interference, some of which could cause the AV to behave in a way that endangers the safety of other road users.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Five thousand dollars is the maximum penalty for the offence and the Courts will be able to calibrate the actual fine to the severity of the circumstances and consequences of any offence or accident.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Thomas Chua, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Henry Kwek raised concerns that the advent of new technologies like AVs and private hire cars may disrupt the livelihood of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This is something that we are equally concerned about.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But as we have all said, rather than impeding the adoption of these technologies, which are beneficial to all Singaporeans, we should focus our efforts on helping our transport workforce adapt to these inevitable disruptions over a 10- to 15-year timeframe.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Together with our unions and companies, we can help our drivers upgrade their skills and perhaps take on higher value and better paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And I am equally happy, like Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, that companies are coming out with novel rental schemes, including dual shifts and hourly rates, so that taxi drivers can be helped with their earnings.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Next, let me address Members' questions on private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Several Members spoke about levelling the playing field between taxis and private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if we will impose Quality of Service standards on private hire car operators.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Louis Ng would like a Code of Conduct to be imposed on private hire car drivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee suggested that we impose a licensing fee on private hire car booking service operators.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This light-touch approach allows the industry, which is still evolving, to continue to innovate and benefit commuters, but also, at the same time, ensures commuter safety.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I believe this is an appropriate approach for now, but we will continue to monitor closely and adjust as needed.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked whether we can allow taxi companies to convert part of their taxi fleets to private hire cars and if we will limit the losses which operators, such as Uber and Grab, can incur.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The role of Government is to put in place an appropriate regulatory framework for businesses to operate.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I do not believe and we should not be taking on the responsibility for their profits or losses as a Government.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Operators must make their own business decisions and the market will impose the necessary discipline over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As for the conversion of taxis to private hire cars, taxi companies today enjoy some concessions which are not applicable to private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: For example, taxi companies today pay the Prevailing Quota Premium (PQP) for Category A vehicles for all their taxis, despite the fact that many of the taxis belong to Category B of the COE system.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Therefore, it would not be right to allow taxi companies to enjoy these concessions on the one hand and then, later, re-registering the vehicle as a private hire car.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why private hire cars must adhere to the child seat rule but taxis need not.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The child seat rule is imposed on all vehicles for safety reasons.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But the Government has allowed a concession for taxis for practicality reasons, as taxis can be street hailed, and it would be quite unreasonable to expect all taxi drivers to ensure that their taxis come equipped with booster seats and child restraints at all times, or to turn away street hail passengers with children.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Private hire cars (PHCs), on the other hand, are pre-booked and passengers can indicate if they require booster seats or child restraints when making the booking.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The Government's exemption of taxis from the child seat rule is the outcome of trying to balance between practicality on the one hand and safety on the other.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah expressed concern over congestion at taxi stands.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Our intent is for taxi stands to remain solely for the use of taxis.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This is also in line with our intent to keep the street hail market solely for taxis.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Hence, in discussing a level playing field, we need to recognise that it would have to be in the total context of not just regulations, but also concessions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Ang Kin Kee raised two questions on the general suspension order.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: First, whether LTA will permanently disallow a PHC booking service provider who has received multiple suspension orders from operating its services.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The suspension order, including the possibility of multiple orders, is a significant regulatory threat which we believe will be sufficient to make service providers take the rules seriously.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We will consider stronger regulation if and when necessary.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Second, Mr Ang asked if LTA will set up a feedback channel to update and inform commuters when a particular PHC booking service operator has been suspended.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: LTA will ensure that sufficient notice and publicity to both drivers and commuters are given before a suspension order commences.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: LTA will study the best channels to do so.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked if such a suspension order may be too harsh given that PHC booking service providers are operating somewhat differently from the taxi industry.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But I would like to assure him that this actually commensurates with the powers that LTA has over other transport service providers today.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: A general suspension order has the same effect as a licence suspension.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Like a licence suspension or revocation, the general suspension order is also a power of last resort to be applied only if they are serious and repeated breaches on our rules.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The affected PHC booking service provider will also be given ample opportunity to present its case to LTA.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Dennis Tan also expressed concerns that it would not be fair for LTA to penalise all drivers affiliated to any particular PHC booking service because of the irresponsible action of a few.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the criteria for PHC Driver's Vocational Licence holders, such as nationality and minimum age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: There are no changes to the criteria announced last year.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And, the number of years of driving experience may, in fact, be more important than age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: When the age was set at 30 for taxi drivers, it was meant to persuade drivers not to take this on early in their life as a permanent vocation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee suggested that the Government ensure that PHC drivers are free to switch platforms whenever they deem necessary.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Agreements between drivers and PHC booking service operators, including the possibility of switching to driving for other operators, should be left as a commercial decision, as per my answer to Mr Yee Chia Hsing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Drivers are advised to carefully read the terms and conditions and ensure that they are fully aware of their rights and obligations, before signing up with an operator.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Perhaps we could suugest that the National Private Hire Vehicles Association may wish to take this up with the various operators.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Louis Ng asked how we would regulate ride-sharing services, such as GrabHitch.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked how we would regulate what seems to be PHC services that ferry school children to and from school.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I believe Er Dr Lee Bee Wah was referring to was Schoolber, which helps parents roster themselves to carpool to send their children to school using their own private cars.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Our regulations allow a driver to use private vehicles to give rides to others travelling to the same destination or in the same direction as himself and for the driver to collect a small fee on a cost-recovery basis, not for profit.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Commuters who are thinking of using such services should assess for themselves their own comfort with the services, in particular, service, including the Chihuahua case.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Over-regulation of this budding initiative will most likely curtail the growth between private arrangements.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: If they are not comfortable with such safety issues or have reservations, they may want to use licensed taxis or PHC services or licensed school bus services, if they are really not comfortable with this pooling service.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin commented that Power-assisted Bicycles (PABs) are similar to lower-powered motorcycles and called for compulsory road safety training for PAB users.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The motor must also be cut off when the user is not pedalling.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: So, if there is no pedalling power, he really cannot get the vehicle to go faster.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In our view, this is more akin to being a bicycle with power assistance.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Thus, we have assessed that we do not need to mandate road safety training for PAB users.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We will continue, of course, to work with the Traffic Police to educate PAB users on safe behaviour and practices, regardless of whether it is more like a motorcycle or more like a bicycle.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about seizure procedures and requirements.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I did not quite get the full query, but I would try and answer to take in all the questions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: LTA has the power to seize PMDs and PABs as long as there are any behavioural offences, such as speeding and reckless driving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: These are offences for seizure, including illegal modifications that do not meet what has been stipulated in terms of the width of the vehicle, the weight of the vehicle and the speed limits structurally placed on the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah expressed concerns that illegally modified private hire cars could pose a danger to the safety of commuters.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We take a very serious view of illegal modifications, whether it is of private hire cars or private cars.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We will continue to ensure that motorists who illegally modify their vehicles are taken to task.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Before I conclude, Mdm Speaker, I just want to address Mr Azmoon's story about him going green.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I applaud that. but the incentives to get more people like the Member to go green would be taken under other initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: It is a balanced stance to ensure commuters' interest, drivers' welfare and business, as many of the Members have raised points about.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Does the Ministry make a difference between a driverless car and an AV?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I do apologise I did not get to that point.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: It is taken into account under the SAE International J3016, where there are different categories of automation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: So, it is a range that we put these vehicles under this framework law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Just a clarification on the last point that the Minister was trying to answer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My question relates to non-compliant power-assisted bicycles as well as the other non-compliant mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For the non-compliant bikes, for example, e-bikes which are supposed to be registered but are not registered.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My question is when these are seen in public, when LTA officers see these devices being used in public, will they be seized or do they have to be committing a separate offence, for example, going at high speed or further illegal modification, in the case of a mobility device?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But as most things operational on the ground, much of the executive judgement is left to the enforcement officers and we will leave it as that.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Sometimes, a person may really not know that he has contravened something and it was done before this law was passed and, for all the different complexities, I will trust the officers on the ground to make the judgement call.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Can we then offer the taxi companies an option where we will let them pay a conversion fee to cover the difference in the COE, as well as any administrative expenses that LTA has incurred to do the conversion?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: One is that taxi companies have already started their own version of PHC, so there is enough market space for them to do the necessary calculations for a viable business model.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: To give them a double benefit, it is premature and probably not the right thing to do either.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: So, for that, we will just leave the space for the businesses to consider their own business models and viability.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Earlier, the Minister mentioned that there is no plan to currently impose licensing fees on private hire operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: It basically has some irony to that because taxi operators have a lot more rules to comply with and there is doubling of their fees.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Whereas now we got to supervise and monitor this group, but there is no fee charged to them and, therefore, other groups have to incur the fees that have to be paid.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Perhaps the Ministry should consider and review this process of not charging the fee on the private hire operators.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I do understand that a licensing fee of 0.01% does not constitute a large proportion.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Like I have said, I take the Member's point.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We can take a look at it and see how a level field can be achieved over time as what we had done last year.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are regular motor vehicles with auto-pilot function considered a subset of autonomous motor vehicles?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If yes, will the eventual insurance that is applicable for autonomous motor vehicles be applicable to this?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The second clarification is on PHC booking service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Private hire car services, such as Uber and Grab, have become a popular mode of point-to-point transport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are fast becoming a reality on our roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In land-scarce and manpower-scarce Singapore, these two disruptive developments carry exciting possibilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They can enhance the efficiency and convenience of our land transportation system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will move us closer towards a car-lite environment, where Singaporeans feel less of a need to own and move around in their own private vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Thus, it is important that we do not impede their growth as some cities have done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On the other hand, we cannot take a completely laissez-faire approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is within this context that MOT is amending the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, we are highly conscious that the advent of these disruptive technologies could have an impact on livelihoods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We cannot and should not stop innovation and progress and I am glad to see that the taxi drivers and companies are rising to the competition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):   Land transportation globally is undergoing an unprecedented digital revolution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Private hire car services have become a popular mode of transport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On the other hand, AVs are fast on their way to becoming a reality on the road, providing another transport option for local passengers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, these two disruptive technologies will enhance the efficiency and convenience of our transport system and they will move us closer towards a car-lite society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOT is now amending the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are adopting a balanced, light-touch regulatory stance that protects the interest and safety of passengers and yet ensures that these technologies have enough space to grow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are highly conscious that the advent of these disruptive technologies could have an impact on some Singaporeans' livelihoods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad to see that taxi drivers and companies are taking these challenges with a positive attitude.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With the widespread deployment of AV technology, the Government will put in place more training programmes to help Singaporeans who drive for a living to acquire new skills and take on higher value-added jobs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, let me now explain the key amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The first set of amendments pertains to AVs in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are set out primarily in clauses 3(a) and 6 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The current Act assumes a human driver to be in control of the vehicle and, thereby, responsible for monitoring the surroundings and making driving decisions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Where automated vehicle technology is installed in a motor vehicle, computer systems control the vehicle, replacing the driver's role.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: AVs thus challenge the very notion of human responsibility which lies at the core of our current road and criminal laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Developers of the autonomous systems must, therefore, provide enough measures to ensure the safe operation of AVs on our general roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The SAE levels of automation are commonly used in the motor industry to define and distinguish the various levels of automation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At levels 3, 4 and 5, it is the AV which monitors the driving environment, and the human driver is no longer required to actively monitor the vehicle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The amendments are not meant and not intended to capture vehicles outfitted with just driver assistance systems like cruise control and assisted parking functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To encourage the use of AV technologies here, clause 6 will allow the Minister for Transport to create new rules to more effectively regulate AV trials or the use of AVs on public roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These rules can place time and space limits on these trials, set standards for the design of the AV equipment and impose requirements to share data from the trials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 6 also allows the Minister, through the rules, to address the anomalies that can arise under existing provisions of the Road Traffic Act or its subsidiary legislation which make a human driver responsible for the safe use of a motor vehicle while on a public road.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The rules, therefore, can exempt AVs, operators of AVs and those conducting or participating in trials of AVs from these existing provisions, and also modify the application of specified provisions of the Road Traffic Act or its subsidiary legislation in respect of these vehicles or persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The second set of amendments pertains to the regulation of the private hire car (PHC) industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These can be found primarily in clauses 31 to 35.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: PHC services have been warmly welcomed by commuters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have been finding it easier to get a ride, whether in a taxi or PHC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is to ensure that they are equipped with sufficient knowledge and skills to provide his or her ride-sourcing service safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Together with our existing rules that require PHCs to be licensed as public service vehicles and to have adequate insurance, these measures help LTA better enforce against errant drivers and vehicle owners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: PHC booking service operators, such as Uber and Grab, play an important role in the enforcement of these rules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The amendments will thus require them to put in place robust systems to ensure that drivers with an affiliated agreement with Uber or Grab and the PHC vehicles they use meet our requirements and standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is, if one of its affiliated drivers has been convicted of or accepted composition for certain offences in the course of being an affiliated driver for that private hire car booking service operator, and there are two or more of such cases in the preceding 12-month period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are offences which compromise commuter safety, namely, providing PHC services without a vocational licence; using an unlicensed vehicle to provide the services, or using a PHC that is inappropriately insured.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A general suspension order has serious implications not just for the PHC booking service operator but also for their affiliated drivers, and the Registrar of Vehicles will not take such a step lightly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Bill does set out a due process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But as the safety of passengers is paramount, the Registrar has to be armed with such powers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our intent is to apply it to instances where the PHC booking service operator repeatedly makes no attempt to ensure that its affiliated drivers adhere to our laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 35 complements clause 34 by empowering LTA to make rules prescribing the duties and responsibilities of PHC booking service operators, such as ensuring that their affiliated drivers hold the appropriate vocational licences and providing LTA with trip and other fleet-related data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The data will help LTA in its transport planning functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our regulations are not overly onerous and I think both Members and service operators like Uber and Grab will agree that these are necessary for the interests of commuters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Currently, the maximum composition sum that can be offered under the Act is $500, regardless of the severity of the offence or the maximum fine prescribed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 27 allows the Courts to mete out both a fine and a jail sentence if a person is found guilty of failing to stop and report an accident that could have occurred due to his vehicle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This change is to ensure that the law is sufficiently deterrent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Next, clauses 13 and 18 empower the Minister to make Rules empowering the Registrar of Vehicles to prohibit the entry and exit of foreign-registered vehicles into and out of Singapore if these vehicles have unpaid charges, including ERP charges, fees or taxes owed to the Singapore Government under the Road Traffic Act and Parking Places Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will improve the effectiveness of enforcement and strengthen deterrence against such foreign vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 45 will amend the Motor Vehicles Third-Party Risk and Compensation Act as a related amendment, to enhance LTA's enforcement against motorists who have been found driving without adequate insurance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, there is a time bar on the prosecution of insurance-related offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: LTA must prosecute someone found driving vehicles with inadequate insurance within either three or six months, after which no prosecution can be made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, this time bar prevents the taking of effective action against offenders in complex cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To prevent circumvention of our vehicle population controls, clause 10 repeals section 12, thus removing the option for Singaporeans and Singapore permanent residents to keep and use foreign-registered vehicles in Singapore simply by paying the requisite Additional Registration Fee (ARF).

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will no longer be allowed to keep or use foreign-registered vehicles in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They strike a balance between such, and safeguarding passengers and other road users' interests and safety.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Breakthrough technology has now made autonomous, or driverless, motor vehicles possible in the not-too-distant future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This House had just last month debated and passed the Active Mobility Bill as we begin to make provisions for the proliferated use of power-assisted bicycles and personal mobility devices (PMDs) on our roads and pathways.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We also have to contend with new private hire car services, such as Grab and Uber, who have entered the point-to-point transportation industry in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This changing transportation landscape requires the Government to review and reconsider our laws and regulations to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The possibility of autonomous or driverless vehicles plying Singapore's roads was raised as early as 2014 when the Committee on Autonomous Road Transport for Singapore (CARTS) was formed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But it was when LTA announced in August last year that it was launching autonomous mobility-on-demand trials that really caught the imagination of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I recall that this was followed by an announcement by nuTonomy, one of the companies that LTA was in collaboration with under the Singapore Autonomous Vehicle Initiative, that it was launching the world's first-ever public trial of a "robo-taxi" service.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This was followed a month later by another announcement of nuTonomy's partnership with Grab, one of Southeast Asia's leading ride-hailing app, to expand its public trial.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I remember following the news with great excitement and anticipation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I felt that this was one of those moments when technology was on the cusp of changing the entire face of transportation, as we knew it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, however, was quickly followed by the first accident involving one of nuTonomy's driverless cars that was on trial.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Thankfully, it was a minor accident where no one was injured.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Separately, a driver of a Tesla car, in the US, driving with its autopilot feature was more unfortunate as he died as a result of an accident with a truck.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Accidents, such as these, will inevitably raise the following questions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Can we trust technology to make the best decision to protect the safety of passengers in AVs?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: How will our infrastructure, roads and transportation networks, which rely primarily on human judgement and decision, assimilate the entrance of such AVs?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: What are the legal implications and liability issues when such AVs are involved in road traffic accidents?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We do have time to answer most of these questions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The technology for AVs remains far from finished.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It will require a significant period of time before AVs become part and parcel of Singapore's transportation landscape.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: AVs, when realised, will bring much efficiency and convenience to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The potential benefits are clear for all to see.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Be that as it may, however, I hope that any eventual implementation of ground-breaking technology, such as AVs, could be done gradually in phases.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is not only to allow for answers to questions, such as those I have raised, but also to manage how such disruptive technologies can affect Singaporeans currently working in transportation industries, such as our taxi drivers and others who drive for a living.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Harsh penalties and strict rules are important to deter irresponsible and reckless users of power-assisted bicycles and PMDs from causing danger not only to themselves, but their fellow road users.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I decided to raise this issue again, this time solely on power-assisted bicycles, primarily because of a recent Straits Times article on certain astute observations that our learned State Coroner made while presiding over fatal accidents involving power-assisted bicycles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the article, it was reported that the learned State Coroner expressed his concern that riders of power-assisted bicycles do not receive any formal training.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He was also noted to have observed that "users of motorised bicycles are subject to particular risks, as these vehicles are capable of attaining high speeds and present a low profile." The Coroner's Court had dealt with a few cases of fatalities resulting from accidents involving power-assisted bicycles and the learned State Coroner would have made his observations based on the facts presented in those cases he presided over.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: His observations and views on this issue are in line with mine.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Any person above the age of 16 is allowed to do so.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am of the respectful and humble view that more can and should be done to rectify this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Doing so will also allow the Traffic Police to monitor irresponsible, reckless and sometimes recalcitrant riders of power-assisted bicycles and take the appropriate action against them, when necessary.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As we encourage more Singaporeans to make use of such modes of transport in our vision for a car-lite Singapore, we can expect such numbers to increase further.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I, therefore, urge the Government to take any further steps as reasonably practical to ensure that we minimise the risks of unfortunate road traffic accidents involving power-assisted bicycles from occurring and to enhance the safety and well-being of all other road users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also seeks to support the move towards paperless vehicle licences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first issue − regulations involving autonomous and driverless vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The car was operated by two test engineers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was reported that "the car knocked into the lorry while changing lanes in Biopolis Drive at one-north".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was also reported that the car belonged to nuTonomy, a start-up software company that is conducting trials of its self-driving vehicles in the one-north business district.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it seems that driverless cars are already being tested without the proposed new regulations in place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, I support the intention of this Bill to provide for a regulatory framework for the undertaking of trials and use on Singapore roads for driverless vehicles and AVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Autonomous or driverless vehicles may well be a sign of things to come.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the eventual regulatory framework has to be tweaked to adapt to its unique features.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In short, the object of regulation and, consequently, the subject of any liability, may, to a significant extent, though possibly not entirely, shift from the driver to the owner of the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope this is still the case as it would be troublesome for other parties in an accident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is any such defect, the present legal regime in law of tort should still apply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is to say, for the owner of the driverless car to seek indemnity from the manufacturer and the other parties involved in the accident should not be expected to take action directly against the manufacturer who may not be based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can also foresee that in cases of accidents caused by or which involve driverless cars, owners may be blaming the vehicle manufacturers and possibly even the suppliers of certain components for the vehicles, including software.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be issues beyond a simple vehicle performance failure, such as failing to do what it is supposed to do, for example, failure to stop when the traffic light turns red.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be more difficult issues of liability which are more subjective or less "black and white", such as reacting to an unexpected course of action by another road user or pedestrian, and avoiding collision or minimising impact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, how will it react to a car driving against the traffic?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the machine react in the same way as we can expect a reasonable driver under our present law?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As SIM senior lecturer in urban transport management, Dr Park Byung Joon, told The Straits Times in a 19 October 2016 article, "humans don't always behave the way they should on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And technology is not advanced enough to pre-empt how humans would behave".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If technology is not able to pre-empt human behaviour in all situations, the law needs to take cognisance of that fact and the regulatory and liability regime must be structured accordingly, so that there is fairness and certainty for everyone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may also be different reactions or reacting time to a similar incident for cars of different manufacturers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is an acceptable reaction that frees its owner from liability or minimise its liability vis-Ã-vis other parties?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will a driverless car be adjudged as failing to keep a proper lookout, a present feature of our law?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will it be subject to the same standard required by our Courts for contributory negligence?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will driverless cars be required to be operated only when a licensed driver is around?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that we may be looking at driverless vehicles performing tasks, such as road cleaning, the answer may be a "no, we don't need a licensed driver or anyone on-board the vehicle at all".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the present situation, any licensed driver is deemed to know the obligations he has to fulfil when an accident takes place while he is behind the wheel, for example, exchange driver's and insurance details.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If driverless vehicles can be operated without the owner or licensed driver, how will the authorities ensure that drivers can obtain access to owner's information of the driverless vehicle?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, if a driverless vehicle can be operated without any person on board or around, how will the owner be informed at the time of an accident so that he can be present to exchange particulars with the driver of the other car or to arrange for his vehicle to proceed with the journey or be sent to a workshop for repairs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the start of driverless driving in Singapore affect the insurance regime and how would it affect insurance claims between driverless cars and normal vehicles?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though the proposed amendments in the Bill today pertain to a regulatory framework for trial purposes and we do not yet have a draft subsidiary legislation for us to study and, hence, we do not know the full details of the proposed regulations, I wonder how the proposed regime will be and how the Government intends to address the issues I have raised which will impact on the regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe we will encounter at least some of these issues even during the trial phase.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, some of these issues may have been encountered by parties in the accident of 18 October 2016 at Biopolis Drive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I, therefore, look forward to the Minister's assurance that these issues that I have raised will be considered in the proposed regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister whether the Government has decided on the requirements for ownership and operation of AVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the new licensing for AVs fall into a separate category requiring additional licensing requirements for existing drivers holding, say, conventional Class 3 licences?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the current Class 3 licence holders be required to attend a further course for AV licensing?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I next move to the issue of private hire car companies providing ride-sourcing services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to know whether this proposed regulation is a result of some serious persistent breaches by any current ride-sourcing company and, if so, what were these breaches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This relates to the forfeiture of seized non-compliant power-assisted bicycles and personal mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, MOT has set out to amend the Bill to encourage innovation as well as to regulate industry players.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, the transport industry has changed drastically with technology innovations and new business models.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Any new development is bound to bring opportunities and challenges.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: And the Government's role, while encouraging innovation and promoting industry development, is to protect consumers' interest and safeguard the rights of related industry players.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, Singapore was the first in the world to test-drive driverless taxis within the city area, and was thus a market leader.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The innovative company picked Singapore for its test drive because of our well-established infrastructure and because drivers and pedestrians observe traffic rules.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Last October, during its test drive, a driverless taxi collided with a lorry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: These amendments will also provide a good example on how to monitor disruptive and innovative technologies in the future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The emergence and the popularity of new technologies will no doubt disrupt original industry practices; be it innovative technologies or new business models, they will upset the social equilibrium.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the Government must protect the public interest first when monitoring the industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of innovative business models, there has been a great breakthrough in the transport industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Traditional taxi services are now facing very intense competition.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Private hire car booking services are flexible and convenient.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: From being disgruntled in the beginning, taxi drivers are gradually getting used to this new model.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In order to get more business, many of them have joined the online taxi booking platforms.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, Uber and Grab have done exceedingly well.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Many users commend on the convenience of their services; but some have reacted negatively.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Convenience lies in people now having a choice between private hire cars and taxis and a higher chance of getting a ride.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Grouses come from the fact that the drivers come from various backgrounds and they may be unfamiliar with the roads and lack relevant experience.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some drivers, in fact, are using their regular working hours to earn a quick buck!

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, plying the same route and using the same booking app, the fares charged by private hire cars are much higher than taxis during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Taxi drivers find this grossly unfair, as too many people are vying for their business and affecting their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is a microcosm of times of change.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: New technologies and business models pose a challenge to traditional industries, forcing everyone to change.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: But in the process of change, social divisions of labour are also changing.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some positions will gradually vanish and the affected workers will have to look for new occupations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I would also like to urge the relevant agencies to safeguard the interest of the current industry players during this transformation period.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Driverless car technologies may solve the problem of manpower shortage in the future and private car booking services may provide more choices to consumers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, we also need to consider the livelihood of taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They rely on driving taxis to support their families.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In Taiwan, Uber was registered as an IT service provider but the authorities thought it belonged to the transport industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The two sides were not able to arrive at a common understanding in terms of oversight.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On one hand, it should take care of consumers' interest and, on the other hand, give space for innovation to grow.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can the policy be considered an ideal one.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I concur with what the Minister has shared; the proposed amendments serve to further enhance the safety for private hire car (PHC) users and, to a certain extent, level the playing field for taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Suspension rules have been in place for commuter safety for a long time.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not an onerous requirement as compared to what other public service vehicles like taxi operators are subjected to.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I was a bit perturbed when, earlier, hon Member Mr Dennis Tan shared that suspension sounds onerous.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But my point is, is not revocation even more onerous?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, the drivers were able to join other taxi operators as there were no anti-competition rules binding them, a point that I will come back to discuss at a later stage.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Steps in the right direction include increasing the safety and reliability of these new commuting options, such as requiring all drivers to be vocationally licensed, go through proper background checks and medical checks as well, be subjected to regulations on insurance adequacy checks and ensuring that their vehicles are approved and licensed to operate as public service vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For now, the onus is not only on the drivers to be properly certified, but also on the service providers who will need to up their game, put in place a robust and rigorous system to ensure that their drivers and vehicles are in compliance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this amendment, I hope to seek two clarifications from the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, will LTA be setting up a feedback channel to update and inform commuters, when a particular PHC booking service provider has been suspended?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will be useful for commuters and tourists to get timely information on the different commuting options and their availability.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will LTA also consider "revoking" their eligibility to operate and not allow them to offer their services to PHC drivers and commuters?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry can also ensure that PHC drivers are not bounded by anti-competition practices.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should have a free market situation whereby a driver can switch company or choose to use whichever platforms he deems suitable or useful to him.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When he leases a car to use for reward and hire purposes, it should not confine him to only using a specific PHC booking service platform.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such an environment will be essential, for example, when a particular booking platform has been suspended and the driver can choose to use other platforms to ensure that his business or livelihood is not affected.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the amendment, I also support empowering LTA to come up with rules and regulations to prescribe the duties and responsibilities of PHC booking service operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The purpose is to align the fees that LTA currently collects from taxi operators for the purposes of transport planning, enforcement, monitoring and related needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, I believe that LTA will need to hire more staff, deploy enforcement officers and lay the necessary groundwork needed to incorporate PHC into its work.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These costs, Madam, I feel, should also be recovered from the PHC operators as well.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is timely that the Road Traffic Act (Cap 276), which is now being proposed to be updated to keep up with the changing automotive landscape not only in Singapore but also with other progressive global cities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Having been involved in the automotive industry for more than 30 years, I can safely say that the changes in the automotive industry are only the beginning, if not more has yet to come.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In supporting the Bill, I would like to highlight two points, which I believe we need to give further attention to, namely: AVs and also in relation to the automated vehicle technology; and classification of vehicles as stipulated by the amendment in clause 4.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Before I elaborate further, please allow me to share my personal experience which happened many years ago.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was somewhere in the year 2009/2010 when I was scouting for a new vehicle.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I decided to try something new, which was to switch to an environmentally-friendly vehicle, with the aim to play my part as a responsible world citizen by considering either an electric vehicle or a hybrid.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Cutting the story short, in consequence, I did not proceed with the purchase.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I felt the rule at that time was not somehow in sync with the expectation and the changing automotive landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Glad to say, today, this rule has meanwhile been updated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, not substantial enough, in my view, to motivate the general mass who have decided to own a vehicle to switch to an environmentally-friendly one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I urge the authorities to continue and rigorously review our Traffic Road Act so as to keep up with the changing times and serve what it is meant to be, that is, to protect and serve the interest of all.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A decade ago, AVs were something which we never thought could be a reality in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: At that time, it was more like a science fiction.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, today, AVs are already running on the road in the USA and generally accepted as the new and "in-thing" innovation within the automotive industry.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is also expected to spread into countries and cities within the next decade, where the infrastructure is ready and available.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Being and wanting to be a global city, Singapore has not much choice but to embrace this new development.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I am for the change and moving ahead together with this new development, I also have concerns.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am unsure if our current Road Traffic Act is geared to meet the challenges which this new automotive innovation brings along with it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, not today, but it will be sometime in the future, I presume.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The second question, should we not distinguish the difference between an AV and a driverless vehicle?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have the expertise and the capability to do this?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The fourth question, how do we ensure that the related laws, rules and regulations are put in place so as to ensure that operators, users as well as the public's interests are protected and served, when the unwanted happens?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The last question, in any unwanted situation, like an accident, immediate human attention is always needed.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am not at all suggesting at all that we avoid moving into this new area of development.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: On the contrary, I believe we should engage and prepare ourselves to embrace and manage it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Autonomous driving and AVs will come sooner or later, with its related technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We should take steps and work faster than ever to make our laws, rules and regulations to accommodate this new automotive innovation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Referring to our Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill, I wish to see more proposed changes in future, so that we keep abreast with the new development in the automotive industry and technologies.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I would even suggest that a panel of experts be assembled to engage this new area of development.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The second part of my concern, Mdm Speaker, is that the classification of our motor vehicles has been in force since I can remember.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe there has been good intention in doing this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The categorisation which has been formulated has served us well.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, motor vehicle technologies have changed and improved, for the better.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Citing an example, a 1,000 cc capacity engine motor vehicle designed and manufactured in the 1980s is no longer comparable with the ones today.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A diesel-powered motor vehicle used to be regarded as environmentally-unfriendly.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, with the advancement and introduction of new technologies, new diesel engines which meet the Euro-V requirements can even be "cleaner" and environmentally-friendlier than some petrol-powered motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What I hope is that the service quality will improve, now that there is more competition.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The improvements in service will also go some way in contributing to the Government's car-lite policy as, hopefully, more people will opt for public transport.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, I would like to raise the following questions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Based on the feedback from my residents, they feel that these drivers are too young, whereas, for taxi drivers, they must be, at the minimum, 30 years old.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, is there a revision in this minimum age?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The taxi companies should re-examine their business models.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To the passengers, what they normally consider are speed and fare.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The one who can come the fastest, the better; and the one the cheaper, the better.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To the taxi drivers, there are also two variables to their income ‒ the rental and the taxi fares ‒ and both are fixed by taxi companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another thing is to get rid of all forms of surcharges and, hopefully, by doing all these, it can bring more income or make taxis more competitive so that the taxi drivers' income will not be affected so much.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the Ministry doing to improve certain infrastructure to cope with the higher number of such private hire cars on the road?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will these private hire cars be allowed to use the taxi stands to alight and pick up passengers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If so, many of our taxi stands are often choked with a long line of cabs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, the queue tails back to a turning traffic-light junction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, even other motorists are unable to turn and this results in a traffic snarl.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, it is an almost daily occurrence at the taxi stand at Bugis Junction where taxis queueing to go into the taxi bay cause a tailback and it gets worse with buses and delivery vans all in the line.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most of our taxi stands cater to just three to four taxis and we may need to review future taxi stands when we build them, depending on their location.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We now also know that there are private car operators who are ferrying school children to and from school, in direct competition with school bus operators.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am all for competition so that there is no monopoly for one group of people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But because school children need to be with trustworthy people and safe drivers at all times, we should look into the safety and security of such arrangements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How is the Ministry to regulate this group of car hire operators?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There was talk that Malaysians are coming here to drive these cars while on social visit passes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If it is not allowed, is there enforcement taken and how many such illegal drivers have been prosecuted?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another point I want to raise is the question of illegal modifications of motor vehicles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Ministry will be very strict with cars which are being used for private hire, to ensure that passengers are not exposed to any danger arising from such modifications.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these modifications would allow drivers to drive at very dangerous speeds, putting passengers at risk.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most important is that the insurance for liability may be void arising from modifications.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   MOT is amending the law to regulate the private hire car industry, so that consumers can enjoy higher levels of service and safety.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are a few areas that I hope the Government can pay attention to.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, with more private hire cars on the road, will they be allowed to use taxi stands in the future?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Considering that most taxi stands can only cater to a few taxis, will this affect the traffic condition on the street?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Government plan to increase facilities in this area?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, there was talk that Malaysians holding social visit passes are now coming to Singapore to drive private hire cars.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether there are restrictions on the kind of permit that private hire car drivers must have and how the Government is going to enforce these restrictions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the Government should have strict controls to ensure that private hire cars are not illegally modified because this could affect passengers' safety and insurance coverage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Obviously, we cannot ignore the impact on taxi drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope taxi companies can reduce the rentals and the fares to help their drivers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since Uber and Grab entered the Singapore market in 2013, we have witnessed a shift in commuter behaviour, as well as a great number of people becoming freelance drivers driving private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many tech-savvy commuters have used these mobile apps and, coupled with sweeteners, such as promotional discounts and the absence of midnight surcharge, this development has been good news for commuters.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there are other aspects of the transport ecosystem we have to consider.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many taxi drivers I have spoken to have indicated that their monthly income has taken a hit due to competition from Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of them are not so tech-savvy and are not able to switch to driving Uber or Grab, which requires the use of smart phone features.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As commuters increasingly shift their preference to these private hire car services, the traditional taxi drivers have picked up fewer passengers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many have thrown in the towel and, worse, some are unable to find other jobs as replacement.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, several countries and cities have applied certain restrictions or banned Uber and other similar services due to the severe market disruptions they have caused.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Car rental companies have also lamented that Uber's affiliate, Lion City Rental, is charging lower than traditional market rate.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Backed by large funds, Uber is focusing on growing its market presence with no consideration as to whether its operations are profitable or not.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Despite our preferred stand of adopting a balanced, light-touch regulatory stance that Second Minister Ng Chee Meng has pointed out, our local players, with less financial clout and operating in a much smaller market, have definitely been affected.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe there are good policy reasons to limit the growth of operators, such as Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What if they collapse under the weight of their huge losses only after wiping out our local players?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If that happens, commuters will be the ones who suffer.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should allow more flexibility in our market to adapt to these market disruptions.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I am very happy that LTA has removed the requirement for taxi drivers to clock a minimum daily mileage of 250 km as there is no such requirement for private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another anomaly is that taxi companies have to meet the Taxi Availability standards introduced in 2013 in order to grow their fleet size, which is capped at 2% per annum, but Uber and other private hire car services have increased their fleet size at an aggressive rate without any restriction during this period.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, I would like to explore if it is possible to allow taxi companies to convert part of their taxi fleet into private hire rental vehicles.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will allow for better utilisation of their fleet.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe we have to think about what happens next.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hopefully, we can minimise the impact on taxi companies and their drivers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the implementation of the requirement for drivers to have vocational licence starting from July this year, I am concerned that the number of private hire drivers may fall.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will this cause Uber and other operators to offer even more incentives to their drivers and commuters?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will this affect our traditional taxi companies and their drivers?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am not against competition, but I am sure everyone agrees that competition should be fair.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen how competition can help drive innovation and prevent complacency by the incumbents.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, we hope that sustained competition can help to improve service standards.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we need to be aware of the entire business ecosystem and its effects on all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Singapore continues to experience economic growth and rising levels of affluence, penalties should also rise concurrently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Only then will penalties bring about the right "pain level", have the appropriate punitive effect and continue to be an effective deterrent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, as always, I do hope we do not just focus solely on penalties to shape our behaviours and morals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope all of us can realise that innocent lives may be lost as a result of our reckless actions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also note that obstruction of driverless vehicles will, for the first time, incur a penalty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As driverless vehicles are the inevitable future for the industry and the world is moving steadily ahead with its development, it is only prudent for Singapore laws to facilitate the testing and use of this innovation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This seems to be rather harsh and I would like to ask the Second Minister for the rationale behind this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also commend the timely and much-anticipated move to further regulate the private hire car industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In comparison, the number of Grab and Uber drivers is estimated to be around 25,000.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Adding another 25,000 cars on the road presents real competition for existing taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, we have understood that the private hire car disruption is here to stay and that it, in fact, does provide a valuable service to the Singapore public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have personally experienced being a Grab driver about a year ago and can see how they are a benefit to consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I have met with taxi drivers and understand their concerns and know that their rice bowls are now affected by this increased competition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, the only thing we should do in terms of Government intervention is to ensure fair competition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must level the playing field as much as possible for both groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I believe that even after these changes, the playing field is still not level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, taxi drivers are required by their Code of Conduct to be properly-attired ‒ shirt, dark-coloured pants, covered shoes and so on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such requirements do not seem to be explicit for Grab or Uber drivers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A driver I met just three Sundays ago brought up this point and wanted to make sure we implement the same rules for both taxis and Uber and Grab drivers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another example was highlighted in the media recently when a GrabHitch driver brought his dog to pick up a passenger and the passenger was bitten.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: GrabHitch responded to the media that Grab does not restrict its drivers from bringing their certified pets on board their vehicles, only encouraging them to inform their passengers beforehand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would not happen in a taxi because rules prohibit drivers to bring their dogs into their taxis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
