text: Lastly, we have also heard in the news recently that it is illegal for Uber and Grab private hire cars to ferry passengers under 135 cm without a child seat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The issue here is not whether the child is in a taxi, a Grab or Uber car.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At times, it may even be the same exact car model.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The issue here is safety and the same rules should apply to all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify why this is not the case for the issue of the child seat?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And would the Ministry consider imposing exactly the same rules and requirements for taxi drivers to drivers of private car hires so as to achieve our intended objective of fair competition?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed regulatory sandbox to promote safe trials for AVs is an excellent move.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Automated vehicles will radically alter the face of Singapore and, as Second Minister Ng Chee Meng has shared earlier, offer exciting possibilities for us.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I would like to talk about three issues pertaining to AVs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, actively managing the ethical dilemmas that AVs bring forth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, readying our transportation workers for the road ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Self-driving vehicles have captured the imagination of many.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Naturally, as more trials and adoption have taken place, more accidents have also happened.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My colleagues have talked about them earlier in the House.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Following the Tesla accident, the US government ordered a detailed safety review.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The finding was clear that, even with the increased number of accidents, Tesla's current implementation is considered safer than conventional vehicles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But regardless of how good the technology gets, accidents will continue to happen.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The rest of the world has started moving on this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In August last year, Tesla started collaborating with AXA in Hong Kong and QBE in Australia to offer insurance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because this is an evolving field, we might not get the approach right the first time, but it is far better for us to try something quick and then adjust along the way so that insurance is not a bottleneck for their commercialisation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Second, let me talk about managing the ethical dilemmas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One major dilemma is: how should an automated vehicle decide on whom or what to protect, when an accident is imminent?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This dilemma is commonly expressed in the field of ethics as the "Trolley Problem", where a driver of a broken trolley has to decide between injuring five people right in front of him, or to make a conscious decision to divert the trolley, thereby injuring a bystander, who is innocent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But for AVs, the issue is even more complex.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Which must the vehicle prioritise to protect and why?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Should it be the passengers of the vehicle?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Or the passengers in a conventional vehicle which can potentially react less swiftly?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Or a nearby vulnerable pedestrian, such as an elderly, an expectant mother or a child?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Or an important nearby building, such as a nursery, or a hospital?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is currently no consensus on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Now, as we accelerate the use of AVs in Singapore, it will be wise if we do not abdicate our responsibilities to technologists or the vehicle manufacturers or the insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOT can keep a close tab on international developments on this front and perhaps even convene an ethics panel to deliberate on this important matter.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some might argue that even as an early adopter city-state, it is unlikely that Singapore can influence the global direction on this front.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I think otherwise, because I believe it is reasonable and feasible for us to ask manufacturers to adapt their programming logic to our society's sensibility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to talk about preparing our transport workers for the disruption ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In a noted study, Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne have worked that most workers in transportation and logistics will be deeply impacted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For us in Singapore, it goes beyond taxi, Uber or Grab drivers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It could also impact our delivery workers and even our transportation workers in the ports or airports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we prepare our transportation workers for the road ahead?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And more importantly, when should we start preparing our workers?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad to hear that Minister Ng believes that it will take 10 to 15 years before AVs are fully commercialised, as this will give our people time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, disruptive technologies have a way of surprising others with the pace of adoption.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I think it would be wise for us to identify a few key trigger points along the adoption path when we know that we have to step in in a systematic and deliberate way to help our transportation workers adjust to this brave new world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that MOT is taking a major step in pushing for the regulatory sandbox for AVs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It may take some time for us to find the right formula, but I am confident that we will succeed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I stand in full support of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union, I am heartened to hear the Minister's assurance that the Government will put in place programmes to help Singaporeans who drive for a living, to help them acquire new skills and take on new jobs, should and when AVs are deployed extensively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Union stands ready to work with the Ministry and the LTA to support our transport workers in the transition to a future AVs world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the meantime, I have some questions regarding public safety − safety of the public from AVs, and safety of commuters using private hire car and ride-sharing services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is timely that we develop a framework to regulate the proper use of such vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since last year, LTA has embarked on various trials for autonomous cars and buses in one-north and NTU respectively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is imperative that more R&D be done in the coming years to ensure that these vehicles are safe before we start using such AVs in the public transport and logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the widespread use of AVs may still be a decade or two away, as indicated by the Minister, it is crucial that we focus on ensuring the safety of our public during the initial trials.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the event of an accident involving an AV, will the Ministry be developing and issuing guidelines for other road users on how they should respond and act?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the person or persons in the AV at the time of the accident be liable?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What happens if there is no one in the AV when the accident occurs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another proposed amendment requires the entity carrying out the autonomous vehicle trials to keep records of the sensor data and video footage gathered during the trials and to submit them to LTA when these are requested.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such records may be lost if there are gaps in the process of safekeeping.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only would this minimise the possibility of lost data, it could also help LTA to get a head start in developing subsidiary innovations that leverage self-driving technology.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When AV technology becomes more reliable and trials expand beyond the current defined locations, we can feasibly expect to see AVs being trialled on major thoroughfares, expressways and even possibly during peak hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the potential increase in AVs on our roads, would AVs be subject to Certificates of Entitlement (COEs)?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, let me touch on private hire car and ride-sharing services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I applaud the proposed changes that serve to level the playing field between the traditional taxi industry and the private hire car industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, there seems to be one category of private hire car drivers that has been left out of this Bill, and these are drivers of ride-sharing services, such as GrabHitch and RYDE.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, LTA allows private car owners to carpool and offer ride-sharing services, with the stipulations that drivers cannot charge for profit and are limited to providing a maximum of two rides per day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider expanding the Act to regulate this group of ride-share drivers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We heard earlier from Member Mr Louis Ng of the viral story where a GrabHitch driver had a Chihuahua in the front seat of his car and the dog bit a commuter who was alighting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A similar vocational licence for ride-share drivers, with mandatory background checks, would serve to enhance the safety of our commuters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This mirrors the approach taken towards the taxi industry currently, where taxi operators are taken to task for the collective actions of their taxi drivers, such as meeting the peak-hour taxi availability standards and Quality of Service standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Taxi operators in Singapore have to adhere to LTA's Quality of Service standards, which take into account the conduct of their taxi drivers, the ease of booking a taxi and the overall safety of taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, taxi operators are penalised when too many of their drivers get into accidents and are deemed to have failed the safety component under the Quality of Service framework.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry consider mirroring the Quality of Service standards placed upon taxi operators to the private hire car operators as well?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While Singapore adopts a light-touch regulatory framework for our private hire car industry, we must protect the safety of our commuters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Placing the onus on the private hire car operators to ensure that they recruit and retain safe and responsible drivers will go a long way in achieving this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Bill.
